item.title: Rent has not aged well
item.description:
Rent is a show about mortality haunted by the untimely death of its author, Jonathan Larson. On the eve of the first preview in 1996, he underwent heart surgery but he didn’t survive to see his creation become one of the most enduring hits in musical-theatre history. The producers of Luke Sheppard’s version don’t need reviewers to offer their verdict because the show has a worldwide band of disciples who maintain its bankability. On press night, the loyalists clearly adored what they’d seen.
The script takes the plot of Puccini’s La bohème and transfers it to New York’s East Village in the 1990s where a salon of artistes are facing eviction.

item.title: It’s the season of short ribs
item.description:
I hereby officially declare autumn open! I am picturing myself bedecked with a wreath of perfect autumn leaves. The bright October sun beams down, warming the cool, crisp air. I am dressed in jewel tones – possibly a cloak – and I’m cradling a pumpkin in one arm and holding a leek in the other, my own autumnal orb and sceptre. There are conkers all around.
The reality of autumn is probably more prosaic: an oversized sweatshirt, some gravy smeared up my forearm, and a grimly determined look as I gaze on the pumpkin and leek lying on my chopping board. It’s probably raining. But I am certainly surrounded by conkers, thanks to my small kids.
Still, the feeling is the same: it’s exciting when it’s time to begin cold-weather cooking.

item.title: Marvel’s Wolverine just doesn’t work
item.description:
Grade: B
If you’re the sort of person for whom ‘SNIKT’ – the sound-effect that, by ancient tradition, accompanies the unsheathing of Wolverine’s adamantium claws – is music to the ears, you may have been looking forward to Marvel’s Wolverine. You may, even, have perked up as you saw a poster for it sail by on the side of a bus.
Alas, I’m here to report that it is, if not exactly a dog, not quite a wolverine either. Industry rumour has it that the developers originally hoped to produce an open-world game along the lines of the successful franchises for Spider-Man and Batman. They were thwarted when they realised that the character doesn’t really lend himself to that.

item.title: The anti-Semitic alliance between Restore and the Greens
item.description:
Johann von Leers was one of Goebbels’s most industrious propagandists: 27 books in 12 years, among them Jews Are Looking at You and Jewry and Knavery. After the war he slipped away to Peron’s Argentina and then to Nasser’s Egypt, where he put his skills to work against Israel. ‘Israel is abnormal,’ he said. ‘It must go. It causes trouble.’ All von Leers did was change his vocabulary – ‘Jew’ became ‘Zionist’ and race science gave way to the language of anti-colonialism and anti-imperialism, with the same ideas finding a new audience in the Arab world.
Von Leers converted to Islam and became Omar Amin, reportedly in honour of Haj Amin al-Husseini, the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and a wartime ally of the Nazis.

item.title: Did the Bayeux Tapestry succeed as a tool of Norman propaganda?
item.description:
It makes for a good pub quiz question: what has 632 people, 202 horses, 55 dogs, 41 ships and only six women? Along with the UK’s heatwaves came Bayeux Tapestry fever as the Canterbury Embroidery returned to England for ten months after something approaching a millennial sojourn in France. The British Museum was barely able to cope with the demands on its website for the first tranche of tickets to visit the exhibition.
It is easy to see why. The Tapestry depicts, in an abundance of endlessly fascinating detail, that most famous date in English history: 1066. In popular perception, the doughty Anglo-Saxons narrowly lost to that bastard Duke William and his land-grabbing Normans at the Battle of Hastings, consequently being forced to submit to the Norman yoke.

item.title: Exclusive: work or face benefits ban, Tories tell under-25s
item.description:
Kemi Badenoch, like many in the Labour party, is not sorry to see the back of Keir Starmer. ‘I did not find Starmer an interesting person,’ she says. ‘He never said anything interesting.’ Andy Burnham is a different proposition. ‘Quite interesting,’ she thinks. ‘He has more of a clear sense of who he is politically, which makes him more confident in terms of what he wants to do. But who he is politically is so far removed from who I am politically that I think that there’s a sharper contrast between us.’
We speak in her office in Portcullis House with the Labour conference in full cry in Liverpool. ‘It feels very much like student union people who’ve got older, but they still want to do the stuff that they did in the student union,’ Badenoch says.

item.title: One for hardcore fans: Golden Boy reviewed
item.description:
Golden Boy, written by Clifford Odets in 1937, feels like a Norman Wisdom movie. A talented boxer wants to become a great violinist so he refuses to throw heavy punches in case he damages his fingers. The boxer, Joe, comes from a loving family who urge him to pursue a musical career but he meets a greedy, fast-talking agent, Tom, who promises him wealth and fame in the ring.
To prise Joe away from his family, Tom encourages his adorable girlfriend, Lorna, to use her influence on him. Lorna promptly falls in love with Joe and the romantic triangle adds heaps of conflict to his career as a boxing champ. Josh O’Connor, looking more like a Hungarian philosopher than a streetfighter, brings an arrogant physicality to the role of Joe.
